paper.title: EGFR-targeted drugs and resistance mechanisms in non-small cell lung cancer: Molecular insights and emerging therapeutic strategies.
paper.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis and progression of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with activating mutations serving as key determinants of sensitivity to targeted therapies. The prevalence and spectrum of EGFR mutations are influenced by histology, ethnicity, and environmental factors, encompassing common alterations such as exon 19 deletions and the L858R point mutation, as well as uncommon variants including exon 20 insertions, kinase domain duplications, and other rare substitutions. These molecular distinctions underlie differential responses to first-, second-, and third-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), emphasizing the necessity of precise molecular profiling for individualized treatment selection. Although EGFR TKIs initially produce robust responses, resistance inevitably develops via on-target mutations (e.g., T790M, C797S), activation of bypass signaling pathways, co-occurring genetic alterations, and histologic or phenotypic transformation, challenging long-term disease control. Contemporary strategies to overcome resistance include combination therapies integrating TKIs with MEK, MET, or AXL inhibitors, antibody-based therapeutics, bispecific antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, and emerging multifunctional biologics. Additionally, immunomodulatory interventions and nanotechnology-based delivery systems enhance anti-tumor efficacy while mitigating resistance. Non-invasive monitoring techniques, such as liquid biopsies, circulating tumor DNA profiling, and advanced imaging modalities, enable longitudinal assessment of mutation dynamics and therapeutic response, informing adaptive, precision-guided treatment strategies. This review synthesizes current knowledge on EGFR mutations, resistance mechanisms, and emerging therapeutic approaches in NSCLC, highlighting the integration of molecular, immunologic, and technological modalities to improve patient outcomes and advance precision oncology.
